note: Hand-written Grade 5 Core-word content, layered over the draft so it always wins. Cast is Grade 5's own, derived from its readings: Amal, Nora, Sami, Teacher Yasmin, Leo, Talia, Zara, Noah, Daniel, Maya, Jamal, Hana, Kobi. Sentences are capped at 100 characters and 17 words, which is Grade 5's own measured maximum — the grade teaches text forms, so its examples are prose rather than the short modelling sentences of the lower grades.

abbreviation.childMeaning: A shortened form of a word or phrase.
practiceSentences: The abbreviation for kilometre is km.
What does this abbreviation stand for?
An abbreviation saves space but can confuse a reader.
She wrote the abbreviation in full the first time.
Every abbreviation should be explained once.

acceptance.childMeaning: Agreeing to something, or coming to terms with it.
acceptance.repitchedFrom: grade 8: 'The act of allowing or agreeing to something, often without questioning it' — the trailing clause makes acceptance sound like a failure to think, which is the opposite of what this unit teaches about coming to terms with a loss.
practiceSentences: Her acceptance of the apology ended the quarrel.
What helps a person reach acceptance after a loss?
The club sent a letter of acceptance to every applicant.
Acceptance does not mean you agree with everything.
The fable ends in acceptance rather than revenge.

access.childMeaning: The right or ability to enter or use something.
practiceSentences: Only staff have access to that folder.
Who has access to the server room?
Access to clean water is not universal.
She was given access for one week only.
Access can be granted and taken away.

accompany.childMeaning: To go somewhere with someone, or to happen alongside something.
practiceSentences: An adult must accompany every group on the trip.
Who will accompany you to the station?
Thunder will usually accompany that kind of cloud.
She asked Nora to accompany her on the walk.
Notes accompany each diagram in the handbook.

accordingly.childMeaning: In a way that fits what has just been said.
practiceSentences: The forecast was poor; accordingly, we changed the route.
She read the rules and acted accordingly.
Accordingly, should the meeting move to Thursday?
He knew the risk and prepared accordingly.
The fable ends badly, and the villagers behave accordingly.
accordingly.note: None of the five was a question - the cross-card proofreader's variety check, which no per-word run can see. Re-done. The first attempt at adding the missing question replaced sentence 3 mechanically, without reading the four around it, and the question then echoed a neighbour - 'She read the rules and acted accordingly.' followed by 'Did she read the rules and act accordingly?'. Five of the eight sets came out that way. The question now sits on a sentence no other one covers, and the displaced statement is restored.

acid.childMeaning: A sour substance that can burn or dissolve other materials.
practiceSentences: Lemon juice is a weak acid.
Which acid is used in a car battery?
Strong acid must be handled with gloves.
Acid rain wears away stone over many years.
The class tested each liquid to find the acid.

acknowledge.childMeaning: To admit that something is true.
acknowledge.repitchedFrom: grade 7: 'To accept or admit that something is true, or to recognise that you have received something.' - two senses joined by `or`. The admitting sense is what this unit's discussion and argument work needs.
practiceSentences: She was willing to acknowledge her mistake.
Will he acknowledge that the plan has failed?
Good writing acknowledges the other side of an argument.
He would not acknowledge that anything was wrong.
Acknowledge the source of every fact you borrow.

acute.childMeaning: An angle smaller than a right angle.
practiceSentences: An acute angle is less than ninety degrees.
Which of these angles is acute?
A triangle can have three acute angles.
The roof met the wall at an acute angle.
Acute is sharp; obtuse is blunt.

adaptation.childMeaning: A feature that helps a living thing survive where it lives.
practiceSentences: Thick fur is an adaptation to a cold climate.
Which adaptation helps this plant hold water?
Every adaptation has a cost as well as a use.
The camel's foot is an adaptation to soft sand.
Adaptation happens over generations, not in one life.

adequate.childMeaning: Good enough for what is needed, but no more.
adequate.repitchedFrom: grade 7: 'Good enough for what is needed; sufficient.' - it explains the word with `sufficient`, which is itself a Grade 5 Core word in unit 7, so the definition borrows a word the learner is separately being taught.
practiceSentences: The light was adequate for reading, but only just.
Is one blanket adequate for a cold night?
Her answer was adequate rather than impressive.
We had adequate food for three days.
Adequate is a low bar, not a compliment.

administer.childMeaning: To manage or give out something officially.
practiceSentences: A nurse will administer the medicine.
Who will administer the fund?
The school administers the test every June.
She was chosen to administer the club's money.
It takes two people to administer the survey fairly.

administrator.childMeaning: A person who manages the daily running of an organisation.
practiceSentences: The administrator keeps the school records in order.
Who is the administrator for this department?
An administrator makes the place work without being seen.
She trained as an administrator after leaving school.
The administrator handles every booking.

adviser.childMeaning: A person whose job is to give expert advice.
practiceSentences: The council appointed a legal adviser.
Who acts as adviser to the committee?
A good adviser tells you what you would rather not hear.
She works as a careers adviser at the school.
An adviser suggests; the decision stays yours.

advocate.childMeaning: To speak up publicly in support of something.
advocate.repitchedFrom: grade 8: 'Verb: to publicly support or recommend. Noun: a person who supports a cause.' - the meaning field carries two part-of-speech labels and two definitions, which is a dictionary entry rather than a word card. This unit teaches actions, so the verb is the one it needs. Its sentences also ran to 110 characters, past this grade's cap, and named Idris, who is not in Grade 5's cast.
practiceSentences: She will advocate for a longer lunch break.
Why advocate a rule that costs you something?
A patient speaker will advocate more effectively than an angry one.
They advocate planting trees along every new road.
I advocate starting small and letting success spread.
advocate.note: Sentence 3 read 'A patient advocate wins more support than an angry one.' - `advocate` as a PERSON, on a card whose meaning and part of speech are both the verb.

aggressive.childMeaning: Ready to attack or argue; forceful and hostile.
practiceSentences: An aggressive tone loses an argument you could have won.
Was the dog aggressive or simply frightened?
She replaced the aggressive wording with something calmer.
Aggressive driving causes most of the accidents here.
There is a difference between firm and aggressive.
The plan worked, albeit more slowly than hoped.
She agreed, albeit with some hesitation.
Was the result fair, albeit a disappointing one?
He finished the race, albeit in last place.
The essay is good, albeit a little long.
albeit.note: None of the five was a question - the cross-card proofreader's variety check, which no per-word run can see.

algebra.childMeaning: Maths that uses letters to stand for unknown numbers.
practiceSentences: In algebra, x can stand for any number.
Why does algebra use letters instead of numbers?
Algebra lets you write a rule that always works.
She solved the algebra question in two lines.
Algebra begins where arithmetic stops.

algorithm.childMeaning: A set of steps a computer follows to complete a task.
algorithm.repitchedFrom: grade 8: 'An algorithm is a set of steps or rules a computer follows to complete a task or make a decision.' - it restates the headword, then offers two endings where one will do.
practiceSentences: A recipe is an algorithm you can eat.
What does this algorithm do first?
An algorithm must work for every case, not one.
The search algorithm ranks the results.
She wrote the algorithm out in plain English first.

allocate.childMeaning: To give something out for a particular purpose.
practiceSentences: The council will allocate money for the new path.
How much time should we allocate to each task?
They allocate one seat per family.
She allocated the jobs before anyone could argue.
Allocate the hardest work to the freshest hour.

altitude.childMeaning: The height of something above sea level.
practiceSentences: The plane levelled off at a high altitude.
What altitude does this satellite keep?
Air grows thin at altitude, so breathing is harder.
The village sits at an altitude of 900 metres.
They measured the altitude with an instrument.
The reading stopped altogether after the storm.
How many samples were there altogether?
Altogether, the trip took nine hours.
She was not altogether sure of the result.
The old telescope was altogether too small.

ambassador.childMeaning: A person who represents their country in another country.
practiceSentences: The ambassador attended the opening of the bridge.
Which country does the ambassador represent?
An ambassador speaks for a whole nation.
She was made ambassador at the age of forty.
The ambassador's residence stands beside the park.

ambition.childMeaning: A strong wish to achieve something important.
practiceSentences: Her ambition was to write a book of her own sheeko.
What ambition does the youngest son hold?
Ambition without patience rarely finishes anything.
His ambition grew after he met the visiting engineer.
The tale warns against ambition that forgets other people.

ambitious.childMeaning: Having a strong wish to achieve something difficult.
practiceSentences: The plan was ambitious for a class of ten.
Is that an ambitious target or a realistic one?
She is ambitious about her writing, and works at it.
An ambitious project needs an honest timetable.
Daniel set himself an ambitious reading goal.

antagonist.childMeaning: The character who stands against the main character.
practiceSentences: The antagonist blocks whatever the hero wants.
Who is the antagonist in this legend?
A good antagonist believes they are right.
The antagonist need not be a person at all.
Hunger itself is the antagonist of that tale.
antagonist.note: Sentence 5 read 'Storm and hunger are the antagonist of that tale.' - a plural subject taking a singular complement, and the card teaches the singular.

anticipate.childMeaning: To expect something and get ready for it.
practiceSentences: Good planning anticipates what could go wrong.
Did anyone anticipate this much rain?
She learned to anticipate the questions she would be asked.
A driver must anticipate what other cars will do.
We anticipate finishing before Friday.

anxiety.note: Not a change from the Core-words work — a pre-existing fault in Grade 5's own vocabulary, surfaced by the cast check. Sentence 4 named Theo, who belongs to Grades 2 and 3 and appears nowhere in Grade 5's readings. Replaced with Noah, who does. This word is `reused` and already has audio, so the edit costs exactly one clip to re-record; the narration index marks it stale by itself.
practiceSentences: A small knot of anxiety sat in Amal's stomach as the concert began.
Taking slow, deep breaths can help you calm your anxiety before a test.
Have you ever felt anxiety before speaking in front of the whole class?
"Talking to my mum about my anxiety always makes me feel better," said Noah.
Nora's anxiety melted away when she saw her friends waving at the school gate.

anyhow.childMeaning: In any case; whatever else is true.
practiceSentences: It was late, but she finished the letter anyhow.
Are you coming anyhow?
The bus was full; we walked anyhow.
Anyhow, the decision has already been made.
He had no map and set off anyhow.

anyway.note: Two faults, both in Grade 5's own reused content. Sentence 2 named THEO, who is not in this grade's readings - the sixth stray name found in this grade, after three more Theos, an Idris and an Omar. And sentence 5 was 'They crawled through anyway.', where `they` and `through` both refer to a passage the card never shows. Restated its headword: 'Anyway means despite what has just been said...'.
practiceSentences: Amal raised her hand anyway, even though her voice shook.
Are you going to the fair anyway, Zara?
Grandma Hana felt tired, but she cooked the soup anyway.
I am not sure it will work, but let's try it anyway!
The path looked blocked, so they went round it anyway.
anyway.childMeaning: Despite what has just been said, or in spite of any difficulties.

apparent.childMeaning: Easy to see or understand; obvious.
practiceSentences: It soon became apparent that the file was missing.
Was the fault apparent from the start?
Her relief was apparent to everyone in the room.
For no apparent reason, the screen went blank.
The apparent answer is not always the right one.

applicant.childMeaning: A person who formally asks for a job or a place.
practiceSentences: Every applicant must complete the same form.
How many applicants applied for the post?
The strongest applicant was not the loudest.
Each applicant is interviewed for twenty minutes.
An applicant should read the advertisement twice.

argument.childMeaning: A reason or set of reasons given to support an idea.
argument.repitchedFrom: grade 5 unit 3: 'A reason given to support an idea, or a disagreement between people.' - two senses joined by `or`. This unit teaches presenting and persuading, so the reasoning sense is the one it needs.
argument.note: Its fifth sentence, 'Choosing the wrong register weakens even the most precise argument.', is the SAME SENTENCE that sat on `register` in unit 6 - one line doing duty as a practice example for two different words, in two different units.
practiceSentences: Sami built a strong argument using facts from the report.
Is fear really a good argument for silencing people?
Amal, your argument convinced the whole class.
A good argument survives being disagreed with.
State your argument before you defend it.

argumentative.childMeaning: Writing that sets out to argue for a point of view.
argumentative.repitchedFrom: grade 7: 'Someone who likes to argue or disagree with others' - the PERSONALITY sense. This unit teaches text types and sets the word beside essay, thesis and rhetorical, where argumentative names a kind of writing rather than a kind of person.
practiceSentences: An argumentative essay states a claim and defends it.
What makes this piece argumentative rather than informative?
Argumentative writing must answer the other side.
She chose an argumentative form for the topic.
The argumentative structure suits a debate.

artery.childMeaning: A tube that carries blood away from the heart.
practiceSentences: Every artery carries blood at high pressure.
Which artery is the largest in the body?
An artery has thicker walls than a vein.
You can feel an artery pulse in your wrist.
A blocked artery is a serious matter.
artery.note: Sentence 1 was 'An artery carries blood away from the heart.', word for word the meaning printed directly above it, so the card's first example taught nothing the learner had not just read.

extraSentences: Astronomy asks questions that take centuries to answer.
astronomy.childMeaning: The study of stars, planets and everything else in space.
astronomy.note: Leaned on `scientific`, taught two units later - and opened by restating its own headword, 'Astronomy is the scientific study of...'. Both faults in one line.

atom.childMeaning: The smallest particle of an element that can exist.
practiceSentences: Everything around you is built from atoms.
How small is a single atom?
An atom has a nucleus with electrons around it.
Two atoms of hydrogen join one of oxygen to make water.
No microscope can show you a single atom directly.

authenticate.childMeaning: To prove that someone or something is genuine.
practiceSentences: A password helps authenticate who you are.
How does the system authenticate a user?
Experts were called in to authenticate the painting.
Two steps authenticate the account more safely.
You must authenticate before the file will open.

automatic.childMeaning: Happening by itself, without a person doing it each time.
practiceSentences: The gate has an automatic lock.
Is the reply automatic or written by hand?
Breathing is automatic; you do not decide to do it.
An automatic system still needs checking.
Her reaction was so quick it looked automatic.

automation.childMeaning: The use of machines to do work people once did.
practiceSentences: Automation changed how the factory was staffed.
What tasks does automation handle best?
Automation removes the dull and repeats the exact.
The mill introduced automation ten years ago.
Automation still needs someone to check it.

backup.childMeaning: A spare copy kept in case the original is lost.
practiceSentences: Keep a backup of your work somewhere else.
When was the last backup made?
A backup you have never tested is a hope.
The backup saved a term's worth of writing.
She makes a backup every Friday.

beneficiary.childMeaning: A person who receives help, money or an advantage.
practiceSentences: The village was the main beneficiary of the grant.
Who is the beneficiary of this scheme?
A beneficiary need not have asked for anything.
She named her sister as the beneficiary.
Every beneficiary was written to in advance.

budget.childMeaning: A plan for how money will be earned and spent.
practiceSentences: The class set a budget for the trip.
How much is left in the budget?
A budget is a plan, not a wish.
She kept to the budget by cutting one item.
The council publishes its budget each year.

business.childMeaning: An organisation that makes or sells things for money.
practiceSentences: Her business sells honey from local hives.
How long has the business been trading?
A small business can grow from one good idea.
The business employs four people.
Running a business means keeping careful records.

campaigner.childMeaning: A person who works publicly to change something.
practiceSentences: The campaigner spoke outside the town hall.
What is the campaigner asking for?
A campaigner needs patience more than volume.
She became a campaigner for safer crossings.
One campaigner started with a single letter.

carbon.childMeaning: An element found in every living thing, and in coal and diamond.
carbon.repitchedFrom: grade 2: 'Carbon is part of the name of a gas that trees take in from the air.' - that describes carbon DIOXIDE by way of its name, which is not what carbon is. At Grade 5 the word sits with atom, molecule and compound, where it is an element.
practiceSentences: Every living thing on Earth contains carbon.
Where is carbon found besides living things?
Diamond and coal are both made of carbon.
A carbon atom can join with four others.
Burning fuel releases carbon into the air.

category.childMeaning: A group of things that share the same features.
practiceSentences: A memoir belongs in the non-fiction category.
Which category does this story fall into?
Each category has its own shelf in the library.
Sorting into categories makes a list easier to search.
The prize has a separate category for poetry.

cemetery.childMeaning: A place where people are buried after they die.
practiceSentences: The old cemetery lies behind the church.
How old is the cemetery on the hill?
Names on the cemetery stones tell the village's history.
A cemetery is a quiet place to walk.
The word cemetery is often misspelled with an a.

characterisation.childMeaning: The way a writer shows what a character is like.
practiceSentences: Her characterisation is done through small actions.
What characterisation do the first two pages give us?
Good characterisation shows rather than tells.
The characterisation of the trickster is the tale's best part.
Dialogue is a tool of characterisation.

chronological.childMeaning: Arranged in the order that things happened.
chronological.note: Meaning kept. The Grade 7 sentences ran to 108 characters and were about clothing swaps, garment museums and supply chains.
practiceSentences: The recount describes the day in chronological order.
Would the story work better in chronological order?
A diary is chronological by its nature.
"Present the steps in chronological order," said the teacher.
She organised her journal chronologically to watch ideas grow.

circulation.childMeaning: The movement of blood around the body.
practiceSentences: Exercise improves your circulation.
How long does one round of circulation take?
Cold hands can mean poor circulation.
The heart drives the whole circulation.
Circulation also means how widely a paper is read.

circumference.childMeaning: The distance all the way around a circle.
practiceSentences: Measure the circumference with a piece of string.
What is the circumference of this wheel?
The circumference grows as the radius grows.
She calculated the circumference from the diameter.
A circle's circumference is a little over three diameters.

citation.childMeaning: A note showing where a fact or quotation came from.
practiceSentences: Add a citation for every fact you borrow.
Which citation supports that claim?
A citation names the author and the page.
Without a citation the reader cannot check you.
She missed one citation and had to redo the page.

civilian.childMeaning: A person who is not in the armed forces or the police.
practiceSentences: The airfield is closed to civilian traffic.
How many civilians live in the valley?
A civilian may not enter the base.
She returned to civilian life after ten years.
Civilian clothes felt strange after the uniform.

clarify.childMeaning: To make something clearer or easier to understand.
practiceSentences: Could you clarify the second instruction?
What would clarify this diagram?
One example can clarify a whole paragraph.
She rewrote the notice to clarify the times.
Ask a question if you need to clarify anything.

climax.childMeaning: The most exciting or important point of a story.
practiceSentences: The climax comes when the two brothers finally meet.
Where is the climax of this tale?
Everything before the climax builds towards it.
A climax that arrives too early leaves nothing after.
The climax is short; the resolution follows it.

coherence.childMeaning: The quality of a text whose ideas fit together sensibly.
practiceSentences: The essay lacks coherence between its second and third parts.
What gives a paragraph coherence?
Coherence comes from order, not from long words.
Read it aloud to test its coherence.
Each paragraph added to the coherence of the whole.

cohesive.childMeaning: Holding together well, with the parts clearly linked.
practiceSentences: A cohesive paragraph reads as one thought.
Is the argument cohesive from start to finish?
Linking words make writing more cohesive.
The team became more cohesive after the trip.
A cohesive text does not make the reader jump.

collaborate.childMeaning: To work together with others on the same task.
practiceSentences: Two classes will collaborate on the display.
Why collaborate rather than work alone?
Scientists collaborate across many countries.
They collaborate best when the roles are clear.
Nora and Kobi collaborate on the class newsletter.

combustion.childMeaning: The process of burning, which gives out heat and light.
practiceSentences: Combustion needs fuel, heat and oxygen.
What happens to the fuel during combustion?
Combustion in the engine pushes the piston down.
Without oxygen, combustion stops at once.
The rocket rises on the force of combustion.

commentary.note: Kept as it stands. The Grade 6 sentences are within this grade's cap and use Grade 5's own cast.
practiceSentences: Sami recorded a clear commentary to explain each part of his board.
Why does good commentary describe the action without hiding the facts?
"Keep your commentary calm and precise," Teacher Yasmin coached them.
Maya added a short commentary beside every photograph.
A commentary walks the audience through the evidence step by step.

commerce.childMeaning: The buying and selling of goods on a large scale.
practiceSentences: The port has been a centre of commerce for centuries.
How has commerce changed the town?
Commerce needs roads as much as it needs money.
Online commerce reached the village late.
Commerce and trade mean much the same thing.

committee.childMeaning: A small group chosen to make decisions for a larger one.
committee.note: The only mined sentence was 'Written by the Year 5 Garden Committee' - a byline from the end of a document, not a sentence.
practiceSentences: The committee meets on the first Monday of term.
Who sits on the school committee?
A committee decides on behalf of everyone else.
The committee voted to plant a hedge.
She was elected to the committee last year.

company.childMeaning: A business that makes or sells things.
company.repitchedFrom: grade 5 UNIT 9: 'Company means the presence of another person or animal that keeps you from being alone.' - the COMPANIONSHIP sense, and all five sentences were about a dog, a monkey and not being lonely. This unit teaches commerce, budget, investor and trader, where a company is a business. It came from THIS grade, one unit away - the fourth time that has happened, after reflection (u2), prime (u7) and Grade 4's pressure and life.
practiceSentences: The company employs thirty people.
Which company made this machine?
A company must keep proper accounts.
She started the company with one van.
The company published its results in May.

comparatively.childMeaning: When measured against something else; relatively.
practiceSentences: The winter was comparatively mild this year.
Is that a comparatively small amount?
Comparatively few pupils walk the long route.
The task was comparatively easy once explained.
Comparatively means you must say compared to what.

competitor.childMeaning: A person or team taking part in a contest.
competitor.repitchedFrom: grade 8: 'A competitor is a person or team taking part in a contest against others.' - it opens by restating the headword, and `against others` repeats what contest already says.
practiceSentences: Each competitor wore a number on their back.
How many competitors entered this year?
The youngest competitor finished third.
A competitor may withdraw at any point.
Every competitor shook hands afterwards.

compile.childMeaning: To collect information together into one place.
practiceSentences: She will compile the results into one table.
How long will it take to compile the list?
They compile a report at the end of every term.
He compiled a book of local sayings.
Compile your notes before you begin writing.

composite.childMeaning: A number with more than two factors.
practiceSentences: Nine is a composite number.
Which of these numbers is composite?
Every whole number above one is prime or composite.
A composite number can be broken into factors.
Four is the smallest composite number.

compound.childMeaning: A substance made when two or more elements join together.
compound.repitchedFrom: grade 6: 'Made by joining two or more smaller words or parts together.' - the WORD-FORMATION sense, which belongs in a spelling unit. Here the word sits with atom, molecule and acid, where a compound is chemical.
practiceSentences: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
Which compound forms when iron rusts?
A compound behaves differently from the elements in it.
Salt is a compound, not an element.
The class listed every compound they could name.
It is hard to comprehend a number that large.
Do you comprehend what the rule actually asks?
Reading twice helps you comprehend the argument.
She could not comprehend his reasoning at first.
To comprehend is more than to recognise the words.

compromise.childMeaning: An agreement where each side gives up something.
practiceSentences: They reached a compromise before the bell rang.
What compromise would settle this fairly?
A good compromise leaves nobody entirely happy.
The brothers found a compromise over the land.
Compromise is not the same as giving in.

computing.childMeaning: The use and study of computers.
practiceSentences: She wants to study computing at university.
What is your favourite part of computing?
Computing is more about thinking than typing.
The computing room is open at lunchtime.
Computing has changed every other subject.

condensation.childMeaning: The change from a gas back into a liquid as it cools.
practiceSentences: Condensation forms on a cold glass on a warm day.
What causes the condensation on the window?
Clouds form by condensation high in the air.
Condensation is the opposite of evaporation.
Wipe the condensation away before you read the scale.

conduct.childMeaning: To carry out or organise an activity.
conduct.repitchedFrom: grade 5 unit 2: 'Conduct means to carry out or organise an activity, such as an experiment or a test.' - it opens by restating the headword, and the example clause makes the meaning narrower than the word.
practiceSentences: Scientists conduct careful tests before every launch.
Why do astronauts conduct so many experiments in space?
Nora and Sami conduct a small experiment each week.
The crew must conduct repairs quickly if something breaks.
She will conduct the interview herself.

connection.childMeaning: A link that joins two things or lets them communicate.
practiceSentences: The connection dropped in the middle of the call.
What connection is there between the two events?
A loose connection stopped the whole circuit.
She checked every connection before switching on.
The connection between reading and writing is close.

conscience.childMeaning: The sense inside you that tells you what is right and wrong.
practiceSentences: His conscience would not let him keep the money he had found.
What does your conscience tell you to do here?
Amal's conscience troubled her all week until she owned up.
A clear conscience is worth more than an easy escape.
The fable ends when the merchant finally listens to his conscience.

conscious.childMeaning: Aware of something, and able to think about it.
practiceSentences: She was conscious of every eye in the hall watching her.
Were you conscious of how quiet the room had become?
Sami made a conscious choice to speak more kindly.
The patient stayed conscious throughout the whole journey.
Being conscious of a habit is the first step to changing it.

considerable.childMeaning: Large enough to matter; a good deal of something.
practiceSentences: A considerable amount of rain fell overnight.
Was there considerable damage to the roof?
She showed considerable patience with the beginners.
The task took considerable time and care.
Considerable effort went into the display.

consideration.childMeaning: Careful thought, or care for other people's feelings.
practiceSentences: She showed consideration by keeping her voice low.
What consideration does a good neighbour show?
After long consideration, he changed his answer.
Consideration for others costs nothing at all.
The plan deserves proper consideration before a vote.

consistent.childMeaning: Always behaving or happening in the same way.
consistent.repitchedFrom: grade 8: 'Always behaving or happening in the same way, without contradicting itself.' - the trailing clause is a second, harder idea bolted onto a clear first one.
practiceSentences: Her handwriting is consistent from start to finish.
Are the readings consistent with yesterday's?
Consistent practice beats occasional bursts.
The rule must be consistent for everyone.
His story stayed consistent under questioning.

constructive.childMeaning: Helpful, and meant to improve rather than to knock down.
practiceSentences: Her comments were constructive and easy to use.
What makes criticism constructive?
A constructive suggestion offers a way forward.
Be constructive, even when you disagree.
The meeting was short but constructive.

consult.childMeaning: To ask someone for advice or information.
practiceSentences: Consult the timetable before you set out.
Who would you consult about this?
She consults a dictionary whenever she is unsure.
They consulted the elders before deciding.
Consult more than one source for a fact that matters.

contemporary.childMeaning: Belonging to the present time; modern.
contemporary.repitchedFrom: grade 7: 'Living or happening at the same time; modern.' - two distinct senses joined by a semicolon. The modern sense is the one this unit uses.
practiceSentences: The gallery shows contemporary painting.
Which contemporary writer do you enjoy?
Contemporary music sounds nothing like this.
A contemporary account is written at the time.
The building looks contemporary beside the old church.

contract.childMeaning: A written agreement between two or more people or groups.
contract.note: The inherited meaning ended without a full stop - the SIXTH such across these grades, after cooperate, announce, antonym, determination and ideal.
practiceSentences: Every player signed the team contract before the first match.
What happens if a builder breaks the contract with the town?
The astronauts signed a contract promising to follow safety rules.
"Read the whole contract before you sign anything," Father says.
Our class wrote a homework contract and everyone signed it.

prey.childMeaning: An animal that is hunted and eaten by another.

processor.childMeaning: The part of a computer that does the calculating.

The processor is the smallest important part.

profession.childMeaning: A job that needs long training or study.

profit.childMeaning: The money left after all the costs are paid.

programming.childMeaning: Writing the instructions that tell a computer what to do.

Good programming reads clearly to a person.

pronunciation.childMeaning: The way a word is said.

Her pronunciation improved by reading aloud.
Pronunciation and spelling often disagree in English.

propose.childMeaning: To suggest an idea or plan for others to consider.

protagonist.childMeaning: The main character, whose story the reader follows.

quotient.childMeaning: The answer you get when you divide one number by another.

A larger divisor makes a smaller quotient.

radiation.note: Meaning kept. One Grade 6 sentence was about clean-up crews and containment near a grove - that grade's own material, and nothing to do with this unit.

ratio.childMeaning: A comparison showing how much of one thing there is to another.

recount.childMeaning: A retelling of events in the order they happened.

Write a recount of the sports day for the newsletter.

reflect.childMeaning: To think carefully about something that has happened.

reflection.childMeaning: Light or sound bouncing back off a surface.

regardless.childMeaning: Without being affected by something else.

The rule applies regardless of age.

regulate.childMeaning: To control something so that it works properly.

Who regulates the quality of the water?

Rules regulate the game so it stays fair.

regulation.childMeaning: An official rule made to control how something is done.

Which regulation covers this case?

Every regulation began as somebody's bad experience.

representative.childMeaning: A person chosen to speak or act for a group.
practiceSentences: Each class elects one representative.

researcher.childMeaning: A person who studies a subject carefully to find things out.

resilience.childMeaning: The ability to recover after something difficult.

respiration.childMeaning: How a living thing releases energy from its food.

retrieve.childMeaning: To get something back from where it was left or lost.

rights.childMeaning: Things a person is entitled to by law or by fairness.

salary.childMeaning: A fixed amount paid regularly for a job.

satisfaction.childMeaning: The pleasure of having done or got what you wanted.

scientific.childMeaning: Based on careful study, testing and evidence.

secretary.childMeaning: A person who keeps the records and notes for a group.

The secretary keeps the register up to date.

security.childMeaning: Protection against harm, theft or unwanted access.

Airport security checked every bag.

self-esteem.childMeaning: The regard you have for your own worth.

sensitivity.childMeaning: Being quick to notice and care about others' feelings.

server.childMeaning: A computer that stores and sends information to others.

Shame that leads to change is not wasted.

steam.childMeaning: The hot gas water turns into when it boils.

symbolism.childMeaning: Using an object or image to stand for a bigger idea.

What symbolism does the river carry here?

Not every object is symbolism; sometimes a pot is a pot.

synthesise.childMeaning: To combine several ideas or sources into one whole.

tax.childMeaning: Money people pay to the government to fund public services.

technology.childMeaning: Tools and methods invented to solve practical problems.

theoretical.childMeaning: Based on ideas rather than on practical experience.

toxic.childMeaning: Poisonous, and harmful to living things.

trade.childMeaning: The buying and selling of goods between people or countries.

transform.childMeaning: To change something completely in form or appearance.

trustworthiness.childMeaning: The quality of being someone others can rely on.

ultimately.childMeaning: In the end, after everything else.

validate.childMeaning: To check that something is true or acceptable.
practiceSentences: A second reading will validate the result.
How do you validate a claim you cannot test?
She validated her findings against the records.
Evidence validates an argument; volume does not.
The experiment validated the earlier prediction.

variable.childMeaning: Something that can change, or a letter standing for it.
practiceSentences: In this equation, x is the variable.
Which variable did you change in the test?
Keep every other variable the same.
A variable can take many values.
Temperature was the variable they measured.

variety.childMeaning: A number of different kinds of the same thing.
practiceSentences: The library holds a wide variety of genres.
What variety of texts have you read this term?
Variety in sentence length keeps a paragraph alive.
She grows three varieties of tomato.
A variety of voices makes the debate stronger.

vast.childMeaning: Extremely large in size or amount.
practiceSentences: A vast plain stretched to the horizon.
How vast is the desert to the north?
There is a vast difference between the two drafts.
The library holds a vast collection of maps.
Vast is a stronger word than big, and rarer.

vegetable.childMeaning: A plant such as a carrot or a bean that people eat.
practiceSentences: A carrot is a root vegetable.
Which vegetable grows best in dry soil?
She chopped one vegetable for every colour.
The vegetable garden feeds the whole family.
Vegetable is spelled with three e's and one a.

vehicle.childMeaning: A machine such as a car or lorry that carries people or goods.
practiceSentences: No vehicle may pass the gate after dark.
What vehicle would you take across sand?
The vehicle was loaded before dawn.
A cart is the oldest vehicle of all.
Each vehicle must be checked before the journey.
The rocket must reach a huge velocity to escape Earth.
What velocity does the probe need?
Velocity is speed with a direction attached.
They measured the velocity of the falling weight.
A small change in velocity alters the whole orbit.
velocity.note: Leaned on `particular`, taught two units later.

verse.childMeaning: A group of lines in a poem or song.
verse.repitchedFrom: grade 1: 'Verse means one part of a song or poem.' - correct and written for a five-year-old, and it opens by restating the headword.
practiceSentences: The second verse repeats the opening line.
How many verses does the song have?
Each verse ends with the same refrain.
She learned the first verse by heart.
A verse in a poem is like a paragraph in prose.

virtual.childMeaning: Existing on a computer rather than in the real world.
practiceSentences: They held a virtual meeting across three countries.
Is this a virtual tour or a real one?
A virtual model can be tested safely.
The museum built a virtual copy of the room.
Virtual is not the same as imaginary.

vital.childMeaning: Absolutely necessary for something to work or survive.
practiceSentences: Water is vital to every living thing.
Why is this step vital to the argument?
A vital piece of evidence was missing.
Sleep is vital, not a luxury.
The vital question is who benefits.

volcano.note: Kept as it stands - the Grade 4 sentences are within this grade's cap and use its own cast.
practiceSentences: Scientists watch the volcano closely for smoke and small shakes.
How long has that volcano been quiet and still?
Hot lava poured slowly down the side of the volcano.
"Our model volcano will fizz and bubble," said Adam.
I built a clay volcano for the science fair.

weathering.childMeaning: The breaking down of rock where it lies, by weather.
practiceSentences: Weathering cracks the rock before erosion carries it off.
How does frost cause weathering?
Weathering happens in place; erosion moves the pieces.
The statue's face was blurred by weathering.
Chemical weathering slowly dissolves limestone.

wellbeing.childMeaning: The state of being healthy, comfortable and happy.
practiceSentences: Sleep matters more to wellbeing than most people think.
What helps your wellbeing on a hard week?
The school looks after the wellbeing of every pupil.
Wellbeing is not only about the body.
Time outdoors improves the wellbeing of the whole class.

whereby.childMeaning: By which; through which something happens.
practiceSentences: A method whereby the answer can be checked.
Is there a rule whereby exceptions are allowed?
They agreed a system whereby each class takes a turn.
The process whereby rock becomes soil is slow.
She explained the way whereby the two connect.

wherein.childMeaning: In which; in what place or respect.
practiceSentences: She wrote a report wherein every claim is sourced.
Wherein does the difficulty lie?
She described the system wherein each class votes.
The passage wherein the hero doubts himself is the best.
Wherein lies the difference between the two?
wherein.note: Sentence 1 was 'A report wherein every claim is sourced.' - a noun phrase, not a sentence.

willing.note: Sentence 5 was 'AMAL: Local families now say they are willing to build better fences.' - a SPEAKER-PREFIXED line lifted from a teaching script. The draft tool now rejects that shape when mining candidates; this one predates the filter and was already in the content. Restated its headword: 'Willing means ready and happy to do something.'.
practiceSentences: Talia was willing to stay late to care for the injured animal.
Are the villagers willing to give up using snares?
Sami, thank you for being so willing to help!
The whole class seemed willing to volunteer at the reserve.
Local families now say they are willing to build better fences.
willing.childMeaning: Ready and happy to do something.

wireless.childMeaning: Working without wires, by sending signals through the air.
practiceSentences: The wireless connection reaches the far classroom.
Is the printer wireless?
A wireless signal weakens through thick walls.
Wireless headphones need charging.
The whole building went wireless last year.

yacht.childMeaning: A light sailing boat used for racing or pleasure.
practiceSentences: The yacht leaned hard as the wind rose.
How many people can that yacht carry?
A yacht needs a deep keel to stay upright.
They watched the yacht round the headland.
The word yacht is spelled nothing like it sounds.
